title: Music is universal
description: A 2019 Harvard-led study found music in every one of 315 societies it examined, with lullabies and dance songs everywhere.

facts.text: A Harvard-led study published in Science in 2019 examined ethnographic records of 315 societies and found music in every one of them.
The same 2019 study found that lullabies and dance songs are ubiquitous across the world's societies.

title: Rhythm, melody and harmony
description: Music combines sounds, usually by cultural standards of rhythm (when), melody (which notes in a line) and, in most Western music, harmony (notes at once).

facts.text: Britannica defines music as combining sounds for beauty of form or emotional expression, usually by cultural standards of rhythm, melody and, in most Western music, harmony.
Rhythm is the organization of sounds in time: patterns of long and short sounds over a steady beat.
A melody is a sequence of single notes heard as one coherent line, often the most recognizable part of a piece of music.
Harmony is the sound of two or more notes heard at the same time; notes sounding together form chords, and a three-note chord is called a triad.

title: Sound is vibration
description: Sound is a pressure wave: a vibrating object pushes air into compressions and rarefactions that pass outward through a medium, and cannot cross a vacuum.

facts.text: Sound is a mechanical wave that needs a medium such as air, water or a solid; it cannot travel through a vacuum.
A vibrating object pushes on the air, making compressions (high pressure) and rarefactions (low pressure) that travel outward as a pressure wave.
In a sound wave, air molecules oscillate back and forth along the wave's direction instead of traveling along with it, like a squeeze running down a coiled spring.
The eardrum vibrates from incoming sound waves and passes the vibrations to three tiny bones in the middle ear.

title: The speed of sound
description: Sound crosses about 343 meters of air per second at 20 C, far slower than light, so thunder lags lightning by about 3 seconds per kilometer.

facts.text: Sound travels through air at about 343 meters per second at 20 C.
Light arrives almost at once but sound covers about a kilometer every 3 seconds, so each 3 seconds from lightning to thunder means about 1 km.

title: Pitch is frequency
description: How high or low a note sounds (pitch) is how we hear frequency, the number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz.

facts.text: Pitch is how we perceive frequency: a sound is higher or lower according to how many times per second its source vibrates, measured in hertz (Hz).

title: A = 440 Hz
description: The international tuning standard sets the A above middle C at 440 Hz: agreed in 1939 and confirmed as ISO 16 in 1975, after decades of local pitches.

facts.text: The international standard tuning pitch sets the A above middle C at 440 Hz; it was agreed in 1939 and confirmed as ISO 16 in 1975.
Before 1939 the tuning A varied by place: France's diapason normal set it at 435 Hz, while Britain's Old Philharmonic Pitch was above 450 Hz.

title: The range of hearing
description: Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and with age most people lose the highest pitches first.

facts.text: Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz).
Age-related hearing loss most often affects high-pitched sounds, like a phone ringing or a microwave beeping, while low-pitched hearing is often unaffected.

title: Beat and tempo
description: The beat is music's steady pulse; tempo is how fast it goes, counted in beats per minute or named with Italian terms like adagio and allegro.

facts.text: The beat is the steady pulse listeners perceive in music, the regular unit that divides musical time.
Tempo is the speed of the beat, often counted in beats per minute (BPM); at 60 BPM one beat falls every second, and 120 BPM is twice as fast.
Traditional Italian tempo markings include adagio (slow), andante (at a walking pace), allegro (fast) and presto (very fast).

title: Meter
description: Meter groups beats into regular measures of strong and weak beats, usually in twos or threes; a waltz counts in threes (3/4 time).

facts.text: Meter organizes beats into regular groups called measures or bars; listeners tend to hear beats in groups of two or three, with strong and weak beats.
The waltz is danced in 3/4 time, three beats to a measure.

title: Melodic contour
description: A melody has a contour, the shape it traces as it rises, falls or arches, moving by steps or by leaps.

facts.text: A melody's contour is its overall shape as it rises, falls or arches; melodies move by steps to neighboring notes or by leaps over several.

title: A melody is a pattern
description: People recognize a melody by the relationships between its notes, so it survives new words and a new starting note: one tune carries Twinkle, the alphabet song and Baa, Baa, Black Sheep.

facts.text: The melody of the French song "Ah, vous dirai-je, Maman", first published without words in 1761 by an unknown composer, carries Twinkle, Twinkle, the alphabet song and Baa, Baa, Black Sheep.
Contour and intervals depend on the relationships between notes, not their exact pitches, so most people recognize a melody moved to a new starting note (transposed).

title: Chords and triads
description: A triad stacks three notes, a root, a third and a fifth; C-E-G is the C major triad.

facts.text: A triad is a chord of three notes, the root, third and fifth; traditional Western harmony builds chords by stacking thirds, as in C-E-G, the C major triad.

title: Consonance and dissonance
description: Consonant combinations sound stable, dissonant ones tense; music moves between them, and the preference for consonance depends heavily on what music you know.

facts.text: Consonance gives an impression of stability and rest; dissonance creates tension or clash; music uses both to build and release tension.
Traditional Western theory counts seconds (like two neighboring keys) and sevenths as dissonant, and octaves, fifths, thirds and sixths as consonant.
In a 2016 study, the Tsimane' of the Bolivian Amazon, with little exposure to Western music, told consonant and dissonant chords apart but rated them equally pleasant.
The 2016 study concluded that preferring consonance depends on exposure to Western music and is not innate; American listeners, especially musicians, preferred it most.

title: Major and minor chords
description: Major and minor triads share a root and a fifth; the minor third is one semitone lower (three semitones above the root instead of four).

facts.text: A semitone (half step) is the smallest step on a keyboard, from one key to the very next, black or white; two semitones make a tone.
A major triad has a major third (four semitones) above its root; a minor triad has a minor third (three semitones); both have a perfect fifth: C-E-G vs C-E flat-G.

title: Is minor sad?
description: Hearing major as happy and minor as sad is largely learned: children pick it up around age 6, and it is weak where Western music is unfamiliar.

facts.text: In a 2001 study, 3- and 4-year-olds did not reliably tell happy from sad music; 5-year-olds judged by tempo alone; 6- to 8-year-olds, like adults, used tempo and major/minor.
A 2022 study of 170 people in Papua New Guinea found that hearing major as happier than minor was strongly tied to exposure to Western-style music such as church hymns.
The 2022 study's authors said they could not exclude a small universal effect, but the pattern points mainly to culture.

title: The octave
description: An octave up doubles the frequency (A 440 Hz to 880 Hz); notes an octave apart sound like the same note and share a letter name.

facts.text: An octave is the interval whose higher note vibrates twice as fast as the lower: above the 440 Hz A is an A at 880 Hz, and below it one at 220 Hz.
Notes an octave apart are heard as the same note at a different height, and they share a letter name: after G the letters start again at A.
The octave is a constant in the scales of most of the world's musical cultures.

title: Scales
description: A scale picks notes inside the octave. Western music splits it into 12 semitones and the major scale follows tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone; other traditions use other ladders.

facts.text: A scale is a graduated sequence of notes dividing the octave; what defines it is its pattern of intervals.
Equal temperament, the standard tuning of Western keyboards, divides the octave into 12 equal semitones.
The major scale follows tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone; started on C it gives C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C, the white keys.
Five-note pentatonic scales are found, in different forms, in most of the world's music, including Native American, sub-Saharan African and East Asian traditions and European folk songs.
Many traditions, including Arabic and Indian classical music, use intervals smaller than a semitone, notes that fall between a piano's keys.

title: The staff and clefs
description: Music is written on a five-line staff that works like a graph (up is higher, left to right is time); a clef names the lines.

facts.text: The five-line staff works like graph paper: the higher a note sits, the higher its pitch, and music reads left to right in time, divided by bar lines.
A staff has five lines and four spaces; notes sit on the lines and in the spaces, each position one letter step from the next.
The treble clef, a curly G, marks the second line from the bottom as the G above middle C, so its lines read E, G, B, D, F and its spaces F, A, C, E.
The bass clef, a stylized F, marks the second line from the top as F.
Stacking a treble staff over a bass staff makes the grand staff; middle C sits on its own short line between them.

title: Note values
description: A note's shape gives its length: each value lasts half as long as the one above, so a whole note equals two halves or four quarters.

facts.text: Each note value lasts half as long as the one above it: a whole note lasts as long as two half notes or four quarter notes.
A whole note is an open oval with no stem; a half note is open with a stem; a quarter note has a filled-in head and a stem.

title: The ear sorts pitch
description: Inside the cochlea, hair cells near the wide end respond to high pitches and those toward the center to low pitches, so each pitch has its own place.

facts.text: Hair cells near the wide end of the snail-shaped cochlea detect higher-pitched sounds, like an infant crying; those closer to the center detect lower ones, like a large dog barking.
